subject: Japan's bond record is a Canadian mortgage problem
bodyMarkdown:
If you are renewing a mortgage this fall, the number that sets your quote moved overnight in Tokyo, not in Ottawa. Long-term borrowing costs are climbing worldwide even as hiring slows, and Canada imports that math whether or not the Bank of Canada touches its policy rate again.

## What happened in Tokyo overnight

Japan's 30-year government bond yield hit a record 4.235% on Monday, Reuters reported, as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi opened an extraordinary session of parliament. Investors were waiting to hear how much Tokyo intends to borrow. Takaichi tried to settle them, pledging to keep a lid on annual bond issuance and to calibrate borrowing to tax revenues, interest rates and debt-financing costs. "Fiscal sustainability is obviously a prerequisite in pursuing our 'responsible and proactive' fiscal policy," she said.

So a government promised discipline and got a record yield anyway. Japan matters here out of all proportion to its growth rate, because Japanese pensions and life insurers spent decades as the reliable buyers of long-dated debt issued everywhere else. When a Japanese insurer can collect 4.2% at home, it stops reaching for yield in Toronto or New York.

## Why the long end is selling off everywhere

The US 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.342% last week, its highest since early 2002 and above the 2007 peak, according to Reuters. It eased to 5.175% on Friday after a soft American jobs report pushed traders to trim their bets on another Fed hike this month. That is still a remarkable price for a decade of lending.

Here is the part I find most useful. Inflation expectations are not what is driving this. Ten-year **breakeven inflation**, the gap between ordinary Treasury yields and inflation-protected ones, was 2.36% on Friday, while the real yield on inflation-protected 10-years ran near 2.92%. Investors expect about 2.4% inflation and want nearly 3% on top of it. That extra compensation for locking money up for a decade is the **term premium**, and it is doing most of the work right now.

## The AI build-out is bidding for the same money

Governments are not the only ones issuing. Hyperscaler bond sales reached roughly $220 billion by August 10, and Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle are expected to spend around $750 billion on capital expenditure this year. They used to build data centres out of cash flow. Now they line up in the bond market beside finance ministries, and it costs them more to do it: Reuters reported that median spreads on their short-dated bonds widened to 40 basis points over comparable Treasuries, from 30 last year.

The pool of money willing to lend for ten or thirty years is finite. Drop a few hundred billion of data centre and power financing into it in one year and long money gets pricier for everyone in the queue, the Government of Canada included. The AI trade and the mortgage market are plugged into the same socket now.

## The takeaway

The Bank of Canada has sat at 2.25% through seven straight meetings and decides again on October 28, but your fixed quote was never set by that rate. It comes off the five-year Government of Canada bond, which is back near 3.6%, and Ratehub listed the best high-ratio five-year fixed at 4.34% on Friday. If you are renewing before spring, I would lock a rate hold now and treat anything under 4.5% as a good outcome rather than wait for relief the bond market is not offering. Watch the five-year GoC yield this month, not the overnight rate.
